intuition: Compare neighboring words to learn letter-order rules. Only the first differing letters tell us which letter comes first. Treat each rule as an arrow, then repeatedly choose a letter with no unmet earlier-letter rules. A cycle means the rules cannot form an alphabet.

Compare neighboring words and turn each first mismatch into a directed edge. A valid alphabet is then a topological ordering of these character dependencies. Initialize every observed character, including letters with no discovered edges, so the output describes the whole observed alphabet rather than only constrained letters.

Two failure modes need separate checks. A longer word before its own prefix is impossible regardless of character order. A dependency cycle is impossible because no character in it can come first. Deduplicating repeated edges prevents duplicate evidence from making a correct graph appear artificially blocked.

steps: For words=[wrt,wrf,er,ett,rftt], create vertices for the five observed letters w,r,t,f,e.
Compare wrt with wrf. Their first mismatch is t versus f, giving t→f.
Compare wrf with er to get w→e; compare er with ett to get r→t; compare ett with rftt to get e→r.
Only w initially has indegree zero. Emit w, which releases e, then emit e, which releases r.
Emit r, releasing t. Emit t, releasing f, then emit f.
All five characters were emitted in order wertf. Every adjacent-word mismatch agrees with this alphabet, so return that string.

concept.correctness: An adjacent pair’s first mismatch gives exactly its necessary letter-order rule, while a reversed prefix pair is intrinsically invalid. Any ordering satisfying all those rules orders the entire adjacent-word chain correctly. Removing ready letters constructs such an ordering; if a cycle stalls it, no consistent alphabet can satisfy the contradictory rules.
